title: The View from Within: What Can Embedded Observers (Not) Learn?
authors: Tomáš Gonda, Johannes Fankhauser, Gemma De les Coves
abstract: Physics is usually done from a third-person perspective, as if the world were described from outside. Yet, observers are themselves physical systems within the world they observe. Here, we investigate this tension using a toy model of classical particles. Observers are physical systems characterised by a choice of (i) a manifest variable, whose value constitutes their empirical record, and (ii) ready states, which provide initial information. We ask what such observers (subjects) can learn about the world through interactions that establish a correlation with another system (the object). For each combination of the three types of learning (about the past, the future, or both), manifest variables, and ready states, we determine what the subject can learn. This shows that many subjects face an epistemic horizon---a limitation to what they can learn about the world---even though the model is classical and deterministic. For example, a subject with a complete manifest variable---one whose ontic state is the empirical record---and partial initial information can learn at most half the object's variables, recovering Spekkens' knowledge-balance principle, i.e. an analogue of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. More generally, we find that subjects face more severe epistemic horizons when predicting than when retrodicting, and that learning by repeatable measurements can be more limited than either prediction or retrodiction alone. Our work provides language and tools to study how the first-person perspective can differ from the third-person perspective beyond the toy model studied here, and invites explanations of the inherent uncertainty in quantum theory from the standpoint of embedded observers.
summary: This work develops a formal theory to analyze the knowledge limits faced by an observer who is itself a physical part of the system being observed. By using a classical toy model, the authors demonstrate that fundamental epistemic horizons exist, even when the underlying physics is deterministic. This provides mathematical tools to bridge the gap between objective physical description and subjective, first-person knowledge.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental tension between the third-person (external) view of physics and the first-person (embedded observer) perspective, determining the limits of knowledge acquisition.
main_result: Embedded observers face an inherent 'epistemic horizon' limiting what they can learn, even in classical, deterministic toy models, providing tools to study first-person uncertainty.
method: The authors use a formal framework based on a toy model of classical particles, analyzing learning constraints by mapping physical interactions to mathematical structures like Poisson maps and coisotropic subspaces.
model_or_system: The model uses classical particles described by a symplectic vector space, where observers (subjects) are physical systems characterized by a manifest variable (empirical record) and ready states (initial information).
key_observables: Epistemic horizon, manifest variable, ready states, predictively inaccessible subspace (I_pre), and preparation support (im(beta)).
important_parameters: The type of learning (past/future), the completeness of the manifest variable, and the structure of the measurement interaction.
main_assumptions: The analysis is built upon a 'nomic toy theory' framework, assuming information gathering is equivalent to physical interaction, and relies on symplectic geometry tools.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four components determining epistemic horizons and depict the structure of measurement interactions, showing correlations between subsystems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework of learning constraints, then developing the mathematical tools using symplectic geometry to analyze prediction vs. retrodiction, culminating in the explicit construction of measurement interactions that realize specific knowledge limitations.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, mathematical framework for quantifying the inherent limitations of knowledge acquisition from the perspective of a physical agent, which has deep conceptual implications for quantum measurement theory.
